The son is like the metaphor of two brothers together becoming śramaṇas;
it is like the metaphor of an actor performing various kinds of performances.

(1) The Parable of the Holy King Attaining the Wheel-Treasure and the Parable of the Brahma King’s Longevity.

Once, at Kukkutārāma Monastery, there was an elder bhikṣu who had attained the path of arhatship. He was accompanied by a śrāmaṇera; whenever they went down into the city to wander and observe, his robes and bowl were very heavy, so he had the śrāmaṇera carry them while following behind him.
While on the road, the śrāmaṇera thought to himself:
"All those born into this world do not fail to experience suffering; if one wishes to escape this suffering, what path should one follow?
Having reflected thus:
"The Buddha always praises the bodhisattva as supreme; I shall now resolve to generate the bodhicitta.
As soon as he had this thought, his teacher, perceiving his thoughts through the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, said to the śrāmaṇera, "Bring your robes and bowl here."
The śrāmaṇera took his robes and bowl and presented them to his preceptor. The preceptor said to the śrāmaṇera, "You go ahead.
Just as the śrāmaṇera was walking in front, he again had this thought:

“The path of a bodhisattva involves immense toil and suffering; to beg for one’s head and give it away, or to beg for one’s eyes and give them away—this is an extreme difficulty that is not within my capacity. It would be better to quickly attain arhatship and swiftly escape from suffering.”
The Master, again perceiving his thoughts, said to the śrāmaṇera,
"Carry your robes and bowl and follow behind me.
This he did three times, and the śrāmaṇera was struck with wonder and astonishment, not knowing the Master's intention.
When he arrived at his lodging, he joined his palms and addressed his teacher, inquiring about the meaning of this.
His teacher replied:
"Because you have advanced three times toward the Bodhisattva path, I have likewise pushed you forward three times."
"Because your mind has regressed three times, I place you last.
The reason for this is that the merit of generating the bodhicitta surpasses that of filling the trichiliocosm with arhats."

(2) Once upon a time, there was a Wheel-Turning Sage King who first fathered nine hundred and ninety-nine sons. They were all exceedingly handsome and beautiful, intelligent and wise, and possessed great physical strength; some were endowed with twenty-eight marks, some with thirty marks, and some with thirty-one marks.
At the very end, the only son first entered his mother’s womb, dwelling amidst the impurities of the *malodaka*.

At that time, there were eight classes of powerful spirits and deities who provided service and protection for his mother with music, stringed instruments, and song; the King also issued a decree to his attendants to provide offerings, with various decorations three times greater than usual.
At that time, the people said to the king:

"Your Majesty’s former sons have now all grown to maturity; they are wise and discerning, and their physical forms are exceptionally sublime, yet Your Majesty remains indifferent and has never shown any sign of joy or celebration."
"Now that this one son has only just entered his mother's womb, what extraordinary signs or exceptional provisions have there been?
At that time, the king replied:

"Although my elder sons possess talents surpassing those of men, none yet is capable of ascending the great throne. If my final-born son grows up to maturity, he will surely be capable of succeeding to the great throne."
At that time, the holy king is a metaphor for the Buddha; the various princes are metaphors for those of the two lower vehicles; and the daughter at the end is a metaphor for the bodhisattva.

It is said that although a bodhisattva may be defiled by worldly dust and impurities, as long as they can give rise to the great resolve, they will surely be held in the thoughts of all Buddhas, and devas, nāgas, and spirits will all offer them reverence and affection.

(3) In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there were two brothers who both left the household life to become śramaṇas. The elder brother delighted in observing the precepts and practicing dhyāna; he sought the Way with single-minded devotion but did not favor giving.
The younger brother delighted in practicing giving to cultivate merit, yet he took pleasure in breaking the precepts.

When Śākyamuni appeared in the world, his elder brother encountered the Buddha, left the household life to practice the Way, and immediately attained arhatship. However, he alone was of meager merit; he constantly suffered from a lack of food and clothing. While wandering with his companions to beg for alms, he would always return alone, unsatisfied.

His younger brother was born as an elephant; possessing great strength, he was able to repel enemies and was beloved by the king. The king bestowed upon him fine gold, silver, precious jewels, and necklaces, and granted him several hundred villages as a fief, providing for this elephant with whatever it required.

At that time, the elder brother bhikṣu encountered a period of great famine; he traveled about begging for food for seven days without success, until finally he obtained a small amount of coarse food, barely enough to sustain his life.
Knowing that this elephant had been his brother in a previous life, he went before the elephant, took hold of its ear with his hand, and said to it:
"I and you both share in this transgression."

The elephant then reflected upon the bhikṣu’s words and immediately attained the recollection of his own past lives; seeing the causal conditions of his previous existence, he became sorrowful and ceased eating or drinking.
The elephant calf, filled with fear, went at once to inform the king, saying, "The elephant no longer eats or drinks; I do not know what the reason is.
The king questioned the elephant calf:
"Has anyone previously committed an offense against this elephant?
The elephant cub replied to the king, "No other person was present;
I saw only a single śramaṇa come to the side of the elephant and depart after a short while."
The king immediately dispatched men in all directions to search for this śramaṇa.
Someone found him among the forest trees and brought the śramaṇa before the king. The king questioned the śramaṇa, saying:
"What did you say when you reached my elephant?"
The śramaṇa replied to the king:
"I have nothing more to say; I simply told the elephant:
'Both you and I are guilty indeed.'"

At that time, the śramaṇa related the story of his past-life causes and conditions in detail to the king. The king’s mind was immediately awakened, and he at once released the śramaṇa, allowing him to return to his dwelling.

4. (Four) Once there was a musician who performed various kinds of music and requested a cow from a wealthy householder. The householder had no intention at all of giving it to him, so he said to him:
"If you can perform such diligent music day and night without ceasing for a full year, I shall give you the cow."
The actor replied, "I can. He then spoke again to the host:
"Can you listen? The elder also replied, "I can."
Thereupon, the musicians, hearing this, were filled with joy; they performed their music with single-minded devotion for three days and three nights without ever ceasing or growing weary.
When the elder had grown weary of listening, he immediately commanded his sons and grandsons to lead a cow to them.

This analogy illustrates that for one who practices the Path and cultivates merit, kalpas are not considered distant; the more diligent and earnest one’s practice, the more swiftly the retribution arrives, such that it does not necessarily require the passage of so many kalpas.

(5) Once, there was a bhikṣu who had been expelled; distressed and lamenting, he walked along weeping and shedding tears. On the road, he encountered a ghost, a being who had also violated the law and been expelled by King Vaiśravaṇa.
Then the ghost asked the bhikṣu,
"For what reason are you walking along weeping and wailing?
The bhikṣu replied:

“I have committed an offense against the Saṃgha and have been expelled by the assembly of monks; I have lost all offerings from donors, and furthermore, my evil reputation has spread far and wide. For this reason, I am grieving, lamenting, and weeping.”
The ghost said to the bhikṣu, “I can cause you to extinguish your ill repute and enable you to receive great offerings.
You should simply mount upon my left shoulder; I shall carry you through the air, so that people will see only you and not my body.”
"If you receive a great offering, you should first give it to me.
That ghost immediately carried the bhikṣu through the air above the village where he had previously been expelled.
When the people of the village saw this, they were all struck with wonder and marvel, believing that he had attained the Way;
they said to one another, "The community of monks has acted improperly by unjustly excluding one who has attained the Way."

At that time, the people of the village all went to this monastery to rebuke the assembly of monks; they immediately welcomed this bhikṣu back to reside within the monastery, whereupon he received great offerings.

This bhikṣu, according to whatever clothing, food, or other requisites he obtained, would invariably first give them to the ghost, never violating their original agreement; on another day, this ghost again carried the bhikṣu as they traveled through the air.

Just then, the officials and subordinates of King Vaiśravaṇa saw the ghost-capturing officer and were struck with great terror; they abandoned the bhikṣu and fled with all their might. Consequently, the bhikṣu fell to the ground and died, his body and head shattered and mangled.

This metaphor illustrates that a practitioner should cultivate their own path toward liberation; they should not rely upon the power and influence of others, for once they fall into ruin, they will be no different from those [whom they relied upon].
(6) Once, Maudgalyāyana was with his disciples, descending from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.
On the road, Maudgalyāyana looked up into the void and laughed heartily.
His disciple asked,
"For what reason and by what cause do you laugh?"
Maudgalyāyana replied, "If you wish to know, you must return to the presence of the Buddha and ask him again.
Thereupon, having finished his almsround, he returned to the Buddha's presence, and his disciple asked Maudgalyāyana once more about the meaning of his previous smile. Maudgalyāyana answered:

"I saw in the space above a hungry ghost whose body was extremely large and whose form was hideous. Seven glowing iron balls entered his mouth and passed straight through him; once they had passed through, they returned and re-entered his mouth. His entire body was ablaze with fire as he writhed in agony, falling down in a faint and rising again, only to fall back down once more. It is for this reason that I am laughing."
"It is not only I who see this; the Buddha also sees it.
The disciple asked, "By what causes and conditions does one suffer in such a manner?"
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"You yourself should ask the Buddha, the World-Honored One, about this.
Thereupon, his disciple immediately addressed the Buddha to inquire about the causes and conditions.

Then the Buddha replied, “This hungry ghost was once a śrāmaṇera in a previous life. At a time of extreme famine, when people subsisted on beans, this śrāmaṇera was distributing food to the assembly of monks. When he reached his own teacher, he intentionally gave him seven extra beans. Because of this transgression, he has received such bitter suffering in the body of a hungry ghost.”
The Buddha said:
"I too have often seen this; the reason I do not speak of it is that I fear people will not believe me and thereby incur a most grievous offense.

This metaphor illustrates that when the Buddha teaches the Prajñāpāramitā, the sin of disbelieving and slandering it is heavier than the five heinous crimes (pañcānantarya), resulting in the extreme suffering of the hells.
(7) In the past, immeasurable eons ago, as numerous as the atoms of dust, there was a bodhisattva named Priyamūla who expounded the Mahāyāna amidst a great assembly.

At that time, Mañjuśrī was an ordinary person who left the household life to practice the Way with single-minded dedication and rigorous asceticism. He practiced the twelve dhūtas to bring merit and deliver all beings. On one occasion, while attending a Dharma discourse, he overheard the Bodhisattva Xigan (Joyful Root) expounding the Dharma of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which stated that lust, anger, and delusion are no different from the Way; they are themselves the Way and are also Nirvāṇa.
At that time, Mañjuśrī heard this but did not believe it, so he immediately departed.
He went to the house of a disciple of Nandika and taught him the Dharma of the impurity of foul secretions. The disciple of Nandika then raised an objection, saying:
"That which is non-existent is the reality of dharmas; all dharmas are empty. How could there be purity or impurity?"
The dhūta bhikṣu remained silent and offered no reply; harboring anger within his heart, he eventually became consumed by resentment.

At that time, a disciple of Nandika recited seventy verses in praise of the Dharma of True Reality (dharmatā). Upon hearing a single verse, the bhikṣu’s anger increased onefold; by the end of the seventy verses, his anger had increased seventy times over.

As soon as he had finished reciting the verse, the earth split open and the Avīci Hell manifested itself; the dhūta bhikṣu immediately fell into it, remaining there for immeasurable kalpas until his retribution was exhausted before finally emerging. Only then did he realize that the sin of not believing in the sublime Dharma is truly grave.
Later he became a bhikṣu and devoted himself to study, attaining great wisdom and becoming foremost in the realization of emptiness.

This parable clarifies that when the Buddha preached the Prajñāpāramitā, those who did not believe and instead slandered it may suffer harm in the present, yet will receive great benefit in the future.

(8) Once, in Northern India, there was a master carpenter of great skill who fashioned a wooden woman of peerless beauty. Adorned with garments and ornaments, she was no different from a worldly woman; she could come and go and even serve wine and attend to guests, with the sole exception that she could not speak.
At that time, there was a painter from South India who was also highly skilled at painting. Upon hearing this, the woodworker prepared fine food and drink and invited the painter.

When the painter arrived, he had the wooden woman serve wine and carry food for him from dawn until night. Unaware of her true nature, the painter believed her to be a real woman; his lustful desire became so intense that he could not stop thinking of her.

As the day drew to a close, the carpenter returned to stay the night; he also asked the painter to remain and settled him there. He then had the wooden woman stand by his side and said to the guest, "I have kept this woman here so that you may sleep with her."

Once the host had entered, the wooden woman stood by the lamp; the guest immediately called out to her, but she did not come. The guest thought that because this woman was bashful she would not come, so he stepped forward and pulled her by the hand, only then realizing she was wood. He felt ashamed and said to himself:
"The host has deceived me; I shall take my revenge."

Thereupon, the painter again devised a stratagem: he drew his own likeness upon the wall, dressed in garments no different from those he himself wore, with a rope tied around his neck as if he had hanged himself, and depicted flies on his mouth pecking at him. Having finished, he closed the door and hid himself beneath the bed.

At dawn, the master emerged and, seeing that the door was not yet open, looked inside; he saw only the image of a guest hanging by a rope on the wall. Greatly terrified, the master assumed the man was truly dead, so he broke down the door, entered, and cut the rope with a knife.
Thereupon, the painter emerged from beneath the bed, and the carpenter was deeply ashamed.
The painter then said, "You were able to deceive me, and I have been able to deceive you; our roles as guest and host are now fulfilled, and we owe nothing to one another."
The two men said to one another,
"How can the delusions that deceive worldly people differ from this?
At that time, the two of them, realizing they had been deceived, each abandoned their loved ones and left the household life to practice the Way.

The Story of Kāśyapa’s Previous Life (9): The father of Kāśyapa was named Nyagrodha; he was a native of the kingdom of Magadha and descended from the Brahmin caste. By virtue of the merit accumulated in his previous lives, he was born into this world as one of great wealth. His rare and precious treasures were the foremost in that country, such that even the wealth of the king fell short by a thousandth part compared to his.

The husband and wife were lonely and lacked offspring. Nearby, at the side of their house, there was a tree deity. At that time, because the couple desired a child, they sought the favor of the tree deity, making offerings for three lifetimes without ceasing year after year; yet what they sought remained forever without result. Consequently, the man became enraged and urgently offered his services to the tree deity, declaring:
"I shall serve you with my utmost sincerity for seven more days. If there is still no sign, I shall cut you down, cast you by the side of the main road, and burn you with fire."

Upon hearing these words, the tree spirit was greatly terrified and did not know by what means she might obtain offspring; she immediately went up to inform the Heavenly King Śikhaṇḍin, recounting the circumstances of the matter in detail to him.
The Heavenly King Śikhaṇḍin then took the tree deity to Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and reported what had been told to him.

Śakra immediately surveyed the realm of desire with his divine eye, but found no one capable of becoming that son. Śakra then informed Brahmā, the Heavenly King, and related the matter to him in full detail.
The Brahma King immediately surveyed that realm with his divine eye and saw a Brahmā deity whose life was about to end; he then addressed him, saying:
"You should descend to be born in Jambudvīpa as the son of the Brahmin Nikūladatta of the kingdom of Magadha."
Brahmā replied, "The Brahmins hold many false views; if I were to descend to be born among them, I could not become their son.
Thus the Brahmā King answered.

“O Brahmin, you are a man of great virtue; among the beings of the desire realm, there is no one capable of being your son. If you are reborn there, I shall command Śakra, Lord of the Devas, to protect you so that you do not fall into false views along the way.”
Brahmā said, "Yes, I shall not disobey the holy instruction. Thereupon, Śakra,
Lord of the Devas, immediately returned to the Desire Realm and fully conveyed this intent to the tree deity, who joyfully returned to inform the elder.
"Do not grieve, do not fear, and do not harbor resentment!
Seven days from now, you shall certainly have a son.
Just as he had said, when the seven days were complete, the woman perceived that she was pregnant; after ten months had passed, the child was born, his body golden in color and radiant with light.
The physiognomist divined and said:

"This child possesses great majestic virtue from past blessings; his will and strength are pure and far-reaching, and he does not crave worldly affairs. If he later leaves the household life, he will surely ascend to the Holy Path."

Upon hearing this, his parents were again filled with great anxiety, fearing that as their son grew up he would abandon them to leave the household life. They wondered, "By what skillful means might we restrain him?
Then they reflected further:
"That which is most prized in the realm of desire is beautiful form; we shall select and take for him a girl of exquisite beauty to bind him to her."
When he reached the age of fifteen and his parents wished to arrange a marriage for him, Kāśyapa heard of this and became deeply distressed.
He said to his parents, "My aspiration is for purity; I have no need for a wife."
Kāśyapa repeated his request three times, but his parents answered as they had before. Then Kāśyapa said to his parents:
"I do not seek an ordinary woman to be my wife; only if you can obtain for me a girl of golden-hued complexion, peerlessly beautiful, will I take her."
The reason for this was that they wished to ensure this matter could not be accomplished.

Thereupon, his parents summoned various brahmins and ordered them to travel throughout the kingdom to seek out a girl whose body was golden in color, who possessed all the female characteristics, and who was upright and exceptionally beautiful; only then would they take her as a wife.

Thereupon, the brahmins devised a stratagem and cast a golden goddess whose features were upright and whose radiance was subtle and exquisite. Carrying the divine image, they traveled from country to country, proclaiming in a loud voice:

"Any woman who beholds this golden goddess, pays homage to her, and makes offerings to her shall, when she later marries, obtain an excellent husband; his body will be the color of gold, his appearance most wonderful, and his wisdom peerless."
Among all the women in the villages and towns who heard this proclamation, there were none who did not respond with sincere hearts; they all came forth to welcome him, prostrate, and make offerings.
However, there was one woman whose body was golden-hued and who was exceptionally beautiful and upright; she remained alone in a secluded chamber and refused to come out to welcome him.
The women admonished him, saying, "All those who behold the goddess of gold have their wishes fulfilled; why do you alone not go out to welcome her? He replied:
"My will is secluded and pure; I do not favor other vows.
The women spoke again:
"Even if you have no vow, what harm would there be in looking upon us together for a moment?"
At that time, the women went together with this woman out before the goddess of gold.
Once this woman arrived, her radiance was so bright and pure that it eclipsed the light of the goddess of gold, such that the goddess no longer appeared.
When the brahmins saw this, they returned and reported it to the elder in full detail.

Thereupon, the elder immediately dispatched a go-between to the girl’s family to convey the elder’s intentions. The girl’s parents had previously heard the name of Kāśyapa and, respectfully accepting his proposal, gave their consent.
Upon hearing this, she was deeply distressed and despondent; however, being constrained by her parents and having no other recourse, she eventually went to the house of the elder.

Once there, she met with Kāśyapa; as the two stood facing one another, their wills were each pure and steadfast, and though they were husband and wife, there was no sentiment of affection between them at all.
His wife then made a vow with Kāśyapa:
"I and you shall each occupy separate rooms; we must not come into physical contact.

At that time, the husband and wife each stayed in a separate room. The father, watching for the moment when Kāśyapa went out, secretly sent someone to demolish one of the rooms so that he was forced to share a single chamber with his wife; yet even though they shared the same room, they used different beds.
The father then sent someone again to bring another bed; thus, although the husband and wife shared one bed, the wife made a further vow with her husband:
"When I am sleeping, you must practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*); when you are sleeping, I shall practice walking meditation."

At that time, his wife was lying down with one arm hanging over the edge of the bed when a large venomous snake approached, intending to bite it. Upon seeing this, Kāśyapa felt a heart of compassion; he wrapped his hand in his robe, lifted the arm, and placed it back upon the bed.
He immediately woke up in a startle and, becoming greatly incensed, said to Kāśyapa, "I previously established a pact;
how have you violated it? Kāśyapa replied:
"Your arm has fallen to the ground and a venomous snake was about to bite it; that is why I rescued you, not because I intended to touch you.
The venomous snake remained nearby, and pointing it out, he showed it to her, whereupon his wife finally understood.
Thereupon, the husband and wife deliberated with one another:
"Why do we not leave the household life to cultivate the Way?
At that time, the couple took leave of their parents and together entered the monastic life to practice the Path in the mountains and marshes.
At that time, there was a Brahmin who, leading five hundred disciples, was also dwelling on this mountain. Upon seeing Kāśyapa and his wife, he immediately gave rise to slanderous thoughts, saying:
"The dharma of those who have left the household life requires each to be chaste; how can there be a husband and wife living together in such a manner?"
At that time, Kāśyapa abandoned his wife and, having purchased a finely woven robe with five hundred taels of gold, retired to a separate grove;
his wife then sought refuge with a Brahmin to become his disciple.

The five hundred disciples of the brahmin saw that this woman was of upright appearance and form, yet she engaged in sexual intercourse every day; unable to maintain her self-control, she eventually could no longer endure it and informed her teacher. The teacher then issued a strict admonition to his disciples, commanding them to restrain their desires.

Later, Kāśyapa encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world; upon hearing the Dharma and receiving his transformation, he immediately attained arhatship. Hearing that his former wife was with a brahmin, he brought her to the Buddha.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for her, and she attained arhatship; her hair fell away naturally and the dharma robes appeared upon her body, whereby she became a bhikṣuṇī. She then traveled about to teach and transform others.

It happened that this coincided with a great assembly convened by King Prasenajit, and the bhikṣuṇīs were thus able to enter the royal palace, where they instructed the various ladies-in-waiting to observe the one-day fast (upavāsa).

When the king returned to the palace in the evening, he summoned his various consorts; however, they all claimed they were observing the fast and none were willing to come. The king then became greatly incensed and said to his attendants:
"Who instructed these ladies to observe the fast?"
The messenger replied, "A certain bhikṣuṇī!
The king then summoned her and commanded her to take the place of the queens for ninety days to receive his carnal desires.
All of this is the result of being pursued by the power of past causes, conditions, and vows; therefore, even though they have attained the state of an Arhat, they cannot escape one another.

(10) Once there were two brothers who left the household life to study the Way. The elder brother constantly reflected upon the practice of dhyāna and cultivated the path with single-minded devotion, attaining the fruit of Arhatship and becoming clear and penetrating in the six supernormal powers.
The younger brother constantly thought only of extensive study and great learning; he was fond of selling his reputation for his own glory.
His elder brother frequently exhorted him, saying:
"A human body is difficult to obtain, and the appearance of a Buddha in the world is rare. Now that you have obtained a human body, you should make the most of this time."
The younger brother said to his elder brother, "One must first study extensively and master the Tripitaka to become a capable teacher of men; only then may one practice dhyāna.

The elder brother again proclaimed for his younger brother the profound meaning of impermanence: that once the exhalation does not return, one belongs to the next world. Yet the younger brother stubbornly clung to his original intent and refused to follow the instruction.
Before long, the younger brother fell gravely ill; though dozens of skilled physicians could not provide relief, they knew he was certain to die and departed after briefly abandoning him.
The brother became terrified, realizing he was about to die, and said to his elder brother:
"In the past, out of my foolishness and shortsightedness, I did not follow your instructions. Now, as my life draws to a close, I do not know what path I shall take."

With tears streaming down his face, he repented before his elder brother; not long after, the man passed away, and the brother immediately entered meditative concentration to observe his destination, seeing that he had been conceived in the womb of an elder’s wife.
The elder’s house was adjacent to the monastery; the elder brother frequently visited this household, seeking to become a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in order to deliver his younger brother.

When the elder’s son was only three years old, [the brother] took him as a disciple to practice giving. When he reached four years of age, the wet nurse carried him to the monastery where the teacher resided. The monastery was situated on a mountain, and the path was constructed by piling stones. While the wet nurse was carrying the child, she did not hold him firmly and lost her grip, causing him to fall to the ground. His head struck a stone, the skull burst open, and he died.

As the child was about to die, he conceived an evil thought, resenting that his embrace had not been firm enough to cause this calamity; consequently, driven by anger, he passed away and fell directly into the Great Hell.

The elder brother again entered meditative concentration to observe him; seeing that he had been reborn in hell, he sighed with lamentation, thinking, "This must surely be his end. The sufferings of hell are so agonizing that they are difficult to transcend; even the Buddhas can do nothing about them, let alone I."

This parable refers to a person whose reputation prevents them from practicing meditation, yet who subsequently falls into the evil realms; even the affection of father and elder brother cannot save them.

(11) Rāhula-maṇi was a disciple of Śāriputra. In a former life, he had once stolen food from a pratyekabuddha; because of this transgression, he was born among the hungry ghosts and suffered for immeasurable kalpas.

Having exhausted his existence as a hungry ghost, he was born among humans, where for five hundred lifetimes he suffered the retribution of hunger. In his final body, he encountered a Buddha who was still in the world; he left the household life to study the Way and donned the three dharma robes. As he wandered about begging for food, no one was willing to give him anything, and for five or seven days he obtained nothing at all.
Maudgalyāyana took pity on him and gave it to him with the alms-food he was carrying; as soon as it fell into his bowl, a large bird snatched it away.
Śāriputra then begged for food and offered it to him; as soon as it entered the bowl, it turned into mud.
Mahākāśyapa begged for alms and offered them to him; as soon as he held them toward his mouth, his mouth closed immediately and there was no way for them to enter.

The Buddha then gave him food; by the power of his great compassion, it immediately entered his mouth, and its flavor was extraordinary. Furthermore, the Buddha employed various skillful means to preach the Dharma for him.
At that time, Rāhula heard this sublime Dharma; moved by a mixture of sorrow and joy, he focused his mind in contemplation and attained the path of Arhatship.

(12) (12) There was a dragon that ascended to heaven and sent down a great rain. When the rain fell upon the celestial palaces, it immediately became the seven treasures; when it fell among human beings, it served as nourishment and moisture; but when it fell upon the bodies of hungry ghosts, it turned into a great fire that burned their entire bodies. Though it was but a single rain, the transformations it underwent where it fell were diverse.
These two matters clarify that the various forms of beings have no fixed substance; they arise according to what is evoked by their transgressions and merits.

(13) In a certain foreign monastery, there was a practitioner among the assembly who happened to defecate on the monks' pure ground. Another practitioner, who was prone to great anger, then licked it with his tongue to show it to the others.
Though they wish to expose the faults of others, they do not realize that they themselves find their own mouths loathsome.
This illustrates how those who delight in speaking of the evils of others are like this: they know only to expose the faults of others, yet remain unaware that they are destroying their own conduct.

14 (14) When a lowly person from a foreign land serves a nobleman, wishing to please him, if he sees the nobleman spitting on the ground, they will compete with one another to come forward and tread upon it with their feet.

There was a man who was not very nimble; although he wished to tread upon someone, he could not do so at first. Later, seeing a person of high status about to spit, as soon as the man gathered his saliva in his mouth, the other stepped on his mouth with his foot.
The nobleman asked,
"Do you intend to rebel?
Why did you trample upon my mouth?"
The commoner replied, "I acted out of good intentions; I did not wish to oppose you.
The nobleman asked:
"If you do not turn back, why have you come to this state?

The lowly man replied, "When Your Honor spat, I always intended to tread upon the spittle; however, as soon as it left your mouth, the crowd would always snatch it away from me. Previously, I was never able to reach it, which is why I stepped upon it right here in your mouth."
This analogy illustrates that during a formal debate, one must wait until the meaning has been uttered before raising an objection.
If one raises an objection while the meaning is still in the mouth and the reasoning has not yet been clearly proclaimed, it is like treading upon someone's mouth.

15 (Fifteen). Once, when the Buddha and his disciples entered the city of Śrāvastī seeking alms, they saw by the roadside a pit filled with the filth and refuse of the entire city; all manner of impure things were contained within it. There they saw an old sow leading her piglets, all lying together within that pit of impurity.

At that time, the Buddha smiled, revealing his forty teeth and four canine fangs. From within these four fangs, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the three thousandfold world system and the ten directions. This light then circled the Buddha’s body three times and entered through the crown of his chest.

In the Dharma of all Buddhas, when they wish to speak of the matters of hell, light enters from beneath their feet; when they wish to speak of the matters of animals, light enters from their shoulders; when they wish to speak of the matters of hungry ghosts, light enters from their thighs; when they wish to speak of human affairs, light enters from their navels; when they wish to speak of the matters of the various devas, light enters from their chests; when they wish to speak of the matters of śrāvakas, light enters from their mouths; when they wish to speak of the matters of pratyekabuddhas, light enters from the mark between their eyebrows; and when they wish to speak of the matters of all buddhas and bodhisattvas, light enters from the crown of their heads.

Ānanda saw light enter through the Buddha’s chest and, knowing that the Buddha wished to speak of the matters concerning the devas, immediately knelt down and addressed the Buddha to inquire about its meaning.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Innumerable kalpas ago, there was an elder who lacked any sons; he had only one daughter who was upright, exquisite, intelligent, and eloquent, and her parents cherished her deeply.”
When the girl had grown up, she spoke a verse to her parents, asking:
"All swift-flowing waters and all matters of suffering and joy in the world—from where do they originally arise, and when shall they ever come to rest?"
When her parents heard this, they marveled at its extraordinary elegance;
not knowing what words to use to answer this verse, the daughter, wishing to understand its meaning yet receiving no reply, became deeply distressed and ceased eating or drinking.

When the parents saw their daughter so distressed and sorrowful, they were seized with great terror; they immediately prepared a grand assembly, inviting various brahmins and wise elders, until the multitude gathered like clouds.

When the offerings had been completed, he provided a small seat within the assembly; the woman sat upon it and repeated the previous verse to question the multitude. The assembly remained silent, and none were able to answer.
The elder then filled a tray with the seven treasures and issued a proclamation, saying:
"To whoever can provide the answer, this shall be given.
At that time, there was a brahmin of upright appearance but meager wisdom who, coveting the precious jewels, spoke:
"I am able to answer.
When the woman heard this, she immediately spoke a verse to question the brāhmaṇa; yet he could not understand the ultimate meaning of this verse and stated directly:
"This matter simply does not exist at all."
The woman then reflected and immediately attained the concentration of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).
She then exclaimed, "This true Great Teacher has benefited me not a little.
Later, when her life ended, she was reborn in the Heaven of Nothingness; after forty kalpas had passed and she had exhausted the lifespan of that heaven, she came to be born in this world.

The daughter of the elder at that time was this very sow; her heavenly merit having been exhausted and the retribution for her past karma having arrived, she has received the form of a pig in this world.
When this woman originally asked her questions in verse, had she encountered a wise teacher, she could have attained the Way;
yet although she practiced meditative concentration, she lacked wisdom, and once the retribution for that concentration has ended, she will fall back into the evil realms.
16. (16) Once there was a great king who fell gravely ill; for twelve years he did not recover, and none of the great physicians were able to cure him.

At that time, a small frontier kingdom under the rule of a great king had a physician who was highly skilled in treating illnesses. The king summoned him to treat his own ailment, and before long, he received a complete cure.
The king then thought of how to repay this teacher’s kindness and repeatedly dispatched messengers to proclaim an edict throughout that country:

“This teacher has cured the king’s illness; he has performed a great service and deserves a reward. Elephants, horses, chariots, cattle, sheep, fields, houses, male and female servants, and all manner of ornamental articles shall be granted to him.”

The minor king, having respectfully proclaimed the imperial decree, prepared for him a residence consisting of lofty halls and multi-storied pavilions; he provided his teacher with a wife, clothing, food and drink, pearl rings, and ornaments, as well as elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep—all things being fully supplied.
While the teacher was by the king's side, no one spoke; the teacher then reflected:
"I have exerted great effort in treating the king's illness, yet I do not know whether the king will reward me or not."

After several more days had passed, the king’s health was restored; his teacher then requested leave to return to his own country, and the king granted him permission, providing him with a weak horse and tattered riding gear.
The Master sighed with great resentment:
"I have exerted great effort in treating the king's illness, yet the king does not recognize my kindness; failing to provide for me, he has caused me to depart empty-handed."
Following the road, he sighed with grief and harbored this as a lifelong regret.
Upon arriving in his native land, he saw a herd of elephants and asked the elephant-keeper's son, "Whose elephants are these?"
The elephant cub replied, "This is my teacher-elephant.
He then asked the elephant cub again:
“From whom did Master So-and-so obtain this elephant?
The young elephant replied,
“It was obtained as a reward for the service of curing the Great King’s illness.”
Proceeding a short distance further, he saw a group of horses and asked the groom,
"Whose horses are these? The groom replied:
"Master, my horse! Having traveled a short distance further, he saw a herd of cattle and sheep and asked the owner of the herd:
"Whose cattle and sheep are these?"
The shepherd replied, "My master owns cattle and sheep.
Continuing forward a short distance, he saw his own original house, which had become a high hall with multi-storied pavilions, vastly different from his former dwelling. He asked the gatekeeper:
"Whose residence is this?
The gatekeeper replied,
"This is the residence of Master So-and-so."
He then entered the inner chamber and saw his wife, her appearance full and joyful, wearing robes of precious jewels; wondering at this, he asked, "Whose wife is she?"
The physician replied, "This is the wife of such-and-such a master.

From the moment he saw the elephants and horses until he entered the inner chambers, he realized that all these things were obtained as the karmic reward for his service in treating the king's illness; he then felt deep regret, thinking that his own efforts in treating the king’s illness had originally been too slight.

This is a metaphor for merit; obstacles to merit are like the king’s illness. The physician is a metaphor for the person who cultivates merit; one who treats the king’s illness is a metaphor for the practitioner who is able to perform meritorious deeds.

The king’s recovery from illness is like the completion of one's merit; the king’s proclamation of rewards—bestowing elephants, horses, and dwellings—signifies that merit is accumulated here while its retribution is realized there.
Generally, those who seek rapid results often suffer from the grievance that the response is delayed.

For instance, a person with little faith may perform meritorious deeds and yet expect a reward by morning or evening; when old age, sickness, and death arrive, they claim that there is naturally no karmic retribution for good deeds. When they attain the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in heaven and wholesome responses fully manifest, it is as if a physician were suddenly to see elephants and horses appear before him.

Having mounted this intermediate state (antarābhava) and reached the celestial palace, one receives the birth-state (upapattibhava) there; seeing with one's own eyes the various adornments of the heavenly realm, one then realizes with regret that in the past one did not perform many meritorious deeds.
It was as if that physician, having received a reward, regretted that his labor in treating the disease had been insufficient.

(17) Once, in a foreign land, there occurred an evil rain; if it fell into the lakes, rivers, wells, moats, or ponds, and people drank this water, it would cause them to become crazed and intoxicated, and they would not recover for seven days.

At that time, there was a king who possessed great wisdom and skill in physiognomy. When clouds arose that portended ill-omened rain, the king perceived this and had a single well covered so that the rain would not enter it.

At that time, the hundred officials and the assembly of ministers consumed the foul rainwater; the entire court went mad, stripping off their clothes and sitting naked upon the royal dais with mud smeared on their heads. Only the king alone did not go mad; he remained dressed in his usual garments, wearing his celestial crown and jeweled necklaces, seated upon his original throne.
All the ministers were unaware that they themselves were mad; instead, they claimed the king was the one who was greatly deranged, asking, "Why is it that you alone are so obsessed?
The people all said to one another, "This is no small matter; let us deliberate together on what is appropriate."
Fearing that his ministers might rebel, the king became terrified and said to them:
"I possess an excellent medicine that can cure this illness; everyone wait a moment while I take it, and I shall emerge shortly."

The king then entered the palace, removed his garments, and smeared his face with mud; he emerged a short while later, and all the ministers, seeing him, were greatly delighted, thinking that such was the proper way of things, unaware that he had gone mad.

After seven days, the ministers regained their senses and were filled with great shame; they each donned their robes and caps and came to the court assembly. The king, however, remained as before, sitting naked.
The ministers were all astonished and asked, "The King is always possessed of great wisdom; for what reason are you thus?"
The king replied to the minister, saying:
"My mind is always settled and undergoes no change; it is because you are mad that you conversely call me mad. Since this is so, it is not my true mind."

The Tathāgata is also like this: because sentient beings have consumed the water of ignorance and are perpetually deranged, if they hear the Great Sage constantly teaching that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, being of one mark which is markless, they will surely claim that the Great Sage is speaking nonsense.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, in accordance with sentient beings, manifests by teaching that these dharmas are wholesome and those are unwholesome, and that these are conditioned and those are unconditioned.
(18) An asura was formerly a poor man who lived near a river and constantly crossed it carrying firewood.

At that time, the river water was deep and its current swift; this man was repeatedly swept away by the water, losing his hold and sinking beneath the waves, yet as he tumbled along with the current, he managed to escape with great urgency.

At that time, a Pratyekabuddha in the guise of a śramaṇa came to the house to beg for food. The poor man joyfully gave it to him; when the meal was finished and the water for washing had been offered, the Pratyekabuddha placed his bowl in mid-air and departed by flying through the sky.
Upon seeing this, the poor man made a vow:
"May my body be so large in my future life that no deep water shall exceed my knees.

By this causal condition, he attained an immense body such that the waters of the four great oceans could not reach his knees; standing in the midst of the great sea, his body surpassed Mount Sumeru, and with his hand resting upon its peak, he looked down at the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
How much more so for the Buddha, who has accumulated great vows over incalculable eons; since his Dharma-body fills all of space, what is there to marvel at?
(19) Once, there was a prince in a certain kingdom who, at the age of seven, entered the deep mountains to seek the way of the immortals, having never known the duties of the court officials.
Later, when the king passed away, there was no one capable of serving as the ruler of the kingdom. The ministers deliberated together, saying:
"The seer in the mountains was originally the prince; moreover, he has cultivated both moral virtue and spiritual power. To appoint him as king would bring benefit to the myriad nations."

The subjects and citizens of the entire realm all went out to the mountain, prostrated before this immortal and installed him as their king; they escorted him back to their own country in a royal carriage and issued an edict for the kitchen officials to prepare exquisite delicacies and sumptuous flavors to feast the Great King.
Because the king found the flavor of the food to his liking, he requested every other item from the kitchen steward. The assembled ministers all laughed and said to the king:

"The duties of the various officials each have their respective domains; the kitchen official is responsible for food, the clothing official for garments, and military affairs and the treasury each have their own administrators. One cannot hold a single person accountable for everything simply because the food was delicious."
This analogy clarifies that each of the various sutras has its own specific subject matter to elucidate; thus, one cannot demand that a single sutra fulfill all requirements.

If that [sutra] elucidates the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, while the Abhidharma elucidates that all phenomena exist and are distinct from one another, it explains them by means of both characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*).
20 (20) The Deer Forest. Formerly, there were five hundred herds of deer in this forest. Among them was a deer king; one was a bodhisattva, and the other was a true deer king.

At that time, there was a king who went out of the city to hunt; seeing this herd of deer, he led his troops to surround them. Those two deer-kings devised a plan together and both went before the human king, kneeling long upon the ground and saying to him:

"We are now within your Majesty’s domain and are destined for slaughter. If Your Majesty were to kill all the deer at once, you could not consume them all before they spoil or rot. We wish to send two deer daily to provide for Your Majesty’s meals; the remainder shall be sent in succession day by day, and we dare not let there be any omission."
"I pray that Your Majesty will grant me leave to extend my life for a short while; would this not indeed be the grace of the Great King?
Thereupon, the king of men granted his request as it had been stated, opening the encirclement and releasing him.
From that time forward, those two deer kings deliberated among themselves and established an order, sending two deer each day to the royal kitchen.
After several more days had passed, there was a pregnant doe whose turn had come to die. That doe went before the king and requested a delay until she had finished giving birth.
The king replied, "The turn of other deer has not yet arrived; who shall take your place?"
The deer then went to where the Bodhisattva king was and said to him:
"My king is unkind and does not exercise reason or forgiveness; I have now come to seek refuge in you, so I pray that you will settle this matter for me."
The Bodhisattva Deer King, pitying him for being in such a state, went of his own accord to the kitchen of the human king. The cook addressed the king, saying:
"The deer king has come to the kitchen himself, seeking to take the place of that pregnant doe."
The king, marveling at this rare occurrence, said to his cook, "Bring that deer king here.
Thereupon, the deer king went to the place of the human king and explained his intention to him in detail; thus, the human king’s faith was born.
"Even birds and beasts still cultivate virtue, how much more so should humans?

He then decreed that within the borders of the entire kingdom, hunting was forever forbidden, and these forests and wilds were granted permanently to the herds of deer; from that time forth, they were named Deer Forest (Mṛgadāva).

21 (Twenty-one). Once there was a householder whose wife was pregnant. After inviting the Buddha to his home and completing the offerings, he wished for the Tathāgata to divine whether the child his wife would later bear would be a boy or a girl.

The Buddha said, "In the future, you shall give birth to a son who will be upright and exceptionally handsome. Upon reaching adulthood, he shall experience celestial joys among human beings, and later he shall attain the path of an Arhat."
When the householder heard this, he was doubtful and did not believe it. Later, after he had again invited the six teachers and completed their offerings, he had them perform a divination.

The householder said to the six teachers, "Previously, I had the śramaṇa Gautama perform a divination, and he said that a son would later be born; I do not know for certain whether it will truly be a boy."
The six teachers said,
"A girl shall be born.
Those six teachers, harboring hatred and jealousy toward the Buddha-dharma, desiring only to act in opposition, reflected within themselves:
"If he gives birth to a son, that householder will surely abandon me and serve the Gautama.
She then spoke these deceptive words:
"Householder!..."

"The wife of your lord shall give birth to a son; however, after the birth of that son, there will be a great calamity, and the family lineage, along with its relatives, will be extinguished for seven generations. Because it is inauspicious, I previously spoke deceptively, saying it would be a daughter."
When the householder heard this, his heart was filled with terror and he did not know what to do.
The six teachers then said to the householder,
"If you wish to attain good fortune and prosperity, you must simply remove it."
The six masters then pressed the abdomen of the householder’s wife, intending by such pressing to cause the fetus to fall.
Although they pressed her repeatedly without success, the householder’s wife subsequently passed away; yet the child did not die, owing to the merit of his past lives.

The layman then abandoned his wife at the place where the corpses were kept, piled up a great heap of firewood, and set her ablaze. When the flames had grown fierce, the Buddha led his disciples to go and observe; the layman’s wife’s body was destroyed, and he saw his son sitting upon a lotus flower, upright and most beautiful, with a countenance as white as snow.
The Buddha commanded Jīvaka:
"Bring this child here.
Jīvaka immediately brought him forth and returned him to his original lay patron; the patron then raised and nurtured him.

When he reached the age of sixteen, his talent and beauty surpassed those of others; he then prepared a great variety of exquisite foods and drinks and invited the six teachers. Once the six teachers were seated, before long, he broke into laughter.
The man asked, "For what reason do you laugh?"
The six masters replied, "We saw a mountain fifty thousand *li* away, with water at its foot; a monkey fell into the water, and that is why we laughed."

The boy, knowing their deception, filled his own bowl with various kinds of fine soup and covered it with rice; he then had someone hold it out to them, while in the bowls of the others, he placed rice at the bottom and soup on top.
Everyone ate, but only the six teachers remained angry and did not eat.
The host asked,
"For what reason do you not eat?"
The six teachers replied,
"Without soup, how can one eat? The host said:
"You can see a monkey fifty thousand *li* away falling into the water with your eyes; why do you not see the soup falling into the rice?
Thereupon, the six masters were greatly incensed; they ultimately did not eat and returned, going straight to Śrīgupta to explain the matter at length.
The man’s elder sister had married Śīlava, and when Śīlava heard of this, he also became enraged. He said to the six teachers:
“Gautama is their teacher; I shall invite our Great Teacher to come and humiliate him.”
For this reason, they prepared a fire pit and poisoned rice.
This parable is extremely extensive; I cannot set it forth in its entirety, so I have briefly cited its essential points.
(22) Once, there was a practitioner who went to the house of a brāhmaṇa to beg for food. The brāhmaṇa had his wife carry the food and feed him, and the wife stood before him.
His wife was beautiful; when the practitioner gazed upon her, his mind immediately underwent a transformation.
He said to the brāhmaṇa, "I wish to depart from the faults and afflictions of sensual flavors. The brāhmaṇa did not understand and asked:
"What is the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding sensual desire?
The ascetic then embraced his wife, kissed her passionately, and said to the Brahmin:
"This is the gratification of sensual desire."
The brahmin became greatly enraged and struck the practitioner once with a staff. The practitioner spoke again:
"This transgression is a source of suffering.
As the brahmin was about to strike him again, the practitioner went outside the gate and turned his head back to say to the brahmin:
"This is an exit. This is a metaphor for how a person cannot profoundly understand the meaning and flavor [of the teaching] unless they must first point to a concrete matter before they realize it.
(23) Once upon a time, there was a country man who visited the capital for a short while. He saw someone being whipped and carrying hot horse dung to smear on their back, and he asked him:
"Why is this so? The man replied,
"It is to ensure that the wound heals easily and leaves no scar."
The countryman kept this secret in his heart; later, upon returning home, he said to his family members, "I have attained great wisdom while in the capital.
Thereafter, his family members asked him:
"What kind of wisdom have you attained?
he asked, and then called out to his servant, saying, "Bring the whip; give me two hundred lashes with it."
The slave, fearing his master and not daring to disobey his command, was immediately whipped two hundred times until blood flowed down his back. The master said to the slave:
"Go and fetch some warm horse dung and smear it on me; this will allow it to heal quickly without leaving a scar."
He said to his family members,
"Do you understand? This is wisdom."

This metaphor refers to a person on the path who has fallen away from the precepts: having originally encountered an enlightened teacher and received the precepts, they immediately attained them; yet upon seeing others receiving the precepts, they abandon their original vows and revert to being laypeople, thereby destroying their Dharma-body.
It is like receiving two hundred lashes until blood flows over one’s back, yet seeking further punishment as if to be smeared with horse dung.

(24) In a foreign land there was a master of dragon-subduing spells; Jūci filled a vessel with water and went to the edge of a dragon pond, reciting the incantation with single-minded focus upon this dragon. Immediately, a great fire rose from the bottom of the pond, and the entire pool burst into flames.

The dragon, terrified by the fire, raised its head to look toward the mountain; it then saw a great conflagration burning the mountains and marshes. Looking up at the mountain peak, he saw it was empty and devoid of any place to dwell. Everything was hot, and there was no ground upon which to escape his body. Seeing only the water within the *muñjā* grass thicket where he could take refuge from the calamity, he extinguished the fire and, assuming a minute form, entered into the *muñjā* thicket.

That dragon pond is a metaphor for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); the mountains and marshes one gazes upon are a metaphor for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); looking at the mountain peak is a metaphor for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); the master of spells who subdues the dragon is a metaphor for the bodhisattva; the water that delays the army is a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*; those incantations are a metaphor for skillful means (*upāya*); the great fire blazing is a metaphor for manifesting impermanence; the dragon’s massive body is a metaphor for arrogance; and its assuming a small form is a metaphor for humility.

It is said that the Bodhisattva manifests the conflagration at the end of an eon, wherein the realms of desire and form are set ablaze; by terrifying sentient beings with this great fire of impermanence, he causes them to eliminate arrogance and become humble and lowly, after which they all enter nirvana.
25 (Twenty-five): Long ago, in a foreign land, there was once a stone by the side of a human path that had been slightly worn down by the treading of carts and horses over a vast period of time.
In that world, there were people who detested its obstruction of the path and were intent on removing it; they struck and destroyed it at once.
They saw a venomous serpent emerge from within the stone, which grew larger upon encountering the wind until, in a mere moment, its body filled the entire Jambudvīpa.
All sentient beings and people within Jambudvīpa would be entirely consumed in a single day before he dies.

This retribution for evil is already so swift; how much more so for a Bodhisattva who, originally a common person, accumulated merit and virtue over kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, and having just resolved his mind, immediately attained the Buddha-way, preached the Dharma to deliver others, and entered nirvana—how could such rapid benefit be considered strange?
26 (26). Once upon a time, there was a snake whose head and tail were quarreling with one another.
The head said to the tail, "I ought to be the superior. The tail replied to the head:
"I, too, should be great.
The head said:
"I have ears that can hear, eyes that can see, and a mouth that can eat; when walking, I am always at the very front. For these reasons, I may be considered great."
"You do not possess this art; you should not consider yourself great.

The monkey said, "It was because I ordered you to go that you were able to leave. Had I encircled the tree with my body for three days without ceasing, your head would have been unable to leave to seek food, and you would have nearly died of hunger."
The head said to the tail, "You may release him; let him become your leader.
Upon hearing these words, the tail immediately released him.
He spoke again to the tail, saying,
"Since you are the largest, you may go ahead. The tail went ahead,
but before he had taken even a few steps, he fell into a fire pit and died.

This is an analogy for when there may be a wise and virtuous Elder among the Saṃgha who is capable of adjudicating the Dharma and Vinaya, yet those below him who are inferior refuse to comply. If the Elder lacks the power to restrain them, he says to them: "Do as you wish."
When an undertaking fails to achieve its aim, both parties fall into what is not the Dharma; it is like that snake falling into a fire pit.

(27) Once there was a bird-catcher who spread a net over a marsh and placed food that birds eat within it. Many birds, calling their companions, vied with one another to eat it. The bird-catcher pulled up his net, and all the birds fell into the net.
At that time, there was a large bird of great strength who lifted up this net and flew away with the flock of birds; the fowler, observing their shadow, pursued them accordingly.
Someone said to the bird-trapper, "The birds fly through the void while you pursue them on foot; how foolish you are!
The bird-trapper replied:
"It would have been better had you told me this; those birds, seeking a place to roost at dusk, were heading in different directions and would thus have fallen.

Yet the man continued to pursue them without stopping. As the day grew ever darker, he looked up and saw the flock of birds flying about, vying with one another—some intending to go east, some west; some looking toward the long forest, others rushing toward the abyss. Thus they did not cease until, in an instant, they fell, and the bird-trapper was finally able to kill them one by one.

The fowler is like Pāpīyān; the spreading of the net is like the fetters (*saṃyojana*); carrying the net while flying is like a person who has not yet abandoned the fetters and seeks the essential path of deliverance; stopping at sunset is like a person whose mind becomes indolent and no longer advances; seeking different roosts is like giving rise to the sixty-two views which are constantly opposed to one another; and the bird falling to the ground is like a person receiving false retribution and falling into hell.
This clarifies that the fetters, afflictions, and defilements are the net of Māra.
(28) (28) Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, there were five hundred strongmen who all became śramaṇas; they dwelt together in one place, practicing dhyāna and reciting the sūtras.
A band of evil thieves plundered all the robes and alms bowls of the śramaṇas, leaving them utterly destitute; only their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robes remained.

After the thieves had departed, the śramaṇas put on those *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robes lightly and went together to the place where the Buddha was, reporting the matter in detail. The Buddha said to the śramaṇas:
"Why did you not cry out loudly?"
The śramaṇas replied: “The Buddha has not yet permitted it; therefore, we did not dare to call him.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If you do not dare to call out, the bandits will strip you of your clothes that very day; who then would be able to provide for you constantly?

From this day forward, I permit you to cry out loudly when you see the bandits coming, and to frighten them away by seizing sticks, bricks, or stones, provided only that you do not intentionally harm them."
That which people value most are their bodies, their lives, and their wealth. These three things are all not to be spared and must not be treated lightly.

They are not to be spared because they are impermanent, subject to ruin, and lack solidity; yet the foolish and deluded cherish them as their own possessions. Through greed, attachment, and stinginess, they give rise to unwholesome causes and conditions, whereby they later fall into the evil realms. Therefore, they are not to be spared.

One must not treat [others] with contempt because they possess a physical body; for by encountering sages and saints, one may rise to receive them, kneel, join the palms, and pay homage, thereby later attaining an indestructible adamantine jewel-body. Therefore, it is said that one must not treat them with contempt.

That life is not to be spared means that because people cling to life, they kill living beings, commit robbery, and engage in sexual misconduct; their speech incurs the four transgressions, and their minds give rise to greed, anger, and false views, whereby they later fall into hell. Therefore, it is said that life is not to be spared.

Furthermore, it should not be taken lightly because, by virtue of destiny, one may encounter sages and worthies, hear the words of the Dharma, and through the penetration of its refined meaning into the divine, practice throughout one's entire life; subsequently, one attains a precious life that is immeasurable and inexhaustible. Therefore, it is said that it should not be taken lightly.

Wealth is not to be begrudged because wealth is the portion shared by the "five families"—namely, thieves, bandits, water, fire, and government officials. When these five suddenly arrive, it may be exhausted in a single instant; therefore, it is said that it is not worth begrudging.

That which must not be treated lightly refers to encountering a virtuous field of merit and using it for almsgiving, making all manner of offerings without any regret or withholding; subsequently, one obtains the four great treasuries of precious wealth, which provide for the destitute and relieve the needy until they are exhausted, thus it is said that it must not be treated lightly.

In cultivating merit and virtue, one should always direct the mind toward seeking the path to Buddhahood; one should not merely seek the retributive fruits of the human or celestial realms. Why is this? It is like planting grain and seeking only its fruit:

although the fruit has not yet ripened, the stalks, joints, branches, and leaves are naturally obtained as well. Cultivating blessings through giving is likewise so: if one resolves the mind and directs one's practice solely toward seeking the path to Nirvana and Buddhahood, then even though that Path has not yet been realized, the joys of the human and celestial realms—including those of a Golden Wheel-turning Sage King, Śakra, and Brahmā—will naturally arrive together. This is just like planting grain and not expecting the stalks, joints, branches, and leaves, yet obtaining them spontaneously.
Therefore, one should not seek only the happiness of the fruits of rebirth as a human or a deva.

(29) Once, in a certain residence in India, there were one hundred thousand śramaṇas; more than fifty thousand had already attained arhatship, their six supernormal powers were perfectly clear, and all outflows were exhausted. The remaining fifty thousand either had attained the three lower paths or had not yet attained them.
There was a householder who, desiring to enjoy the bliss and fortune of humans and devas at will, came to a stupa and temple to provide meals and make offerings to the assembly of monks.

At that time, there was a senior elder (sthavira) who was a great arhat possessing the six supernormal powers; he was extremely old, with white hair and fallen teeth, his physical form withered and decayed, yet he was the foremost among the hundred thousand people present.
When the Elder had finished his prayers of blessing, and the meal was concluded and the water for washing hands had been offered, [the monk] spoke to the Elder, saying:
"Donor! It is only now that your gift incurs a great offense."
At that time, those in the assembly who had not yet attained the Path all said,
"The Elder speaks such delirious words only because he is old. The Elder replied:
"It is indeed so; it is no idle talk.
The crowd asked, "This man has planted blessings; how could he have incurred sin?"
The Elder replied: "You recognize one thing but do not recognize the other.

This person has planted merit and subsequently experienced the pleasures of the human and celestial realms; yet, amidst these pleasures, he became greatly arrogant, considering himself sufficient and seeking no liberation. Seeing the Buddha, he did not pay homage; seeing the sutras, he did not read them; seeing śramaṇas, he had no heart of reverence. Indulging in negligence and self-indulgence, once his store of merit is exhausted, he shall fall into the evil paths for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Only after his transgressions are finished will he emerge. The reason he was able to plant such great demerit is precisely because he received such great worldly retribution."
"If one directs the mind toward the Noble Path while performing this meritorious act, then at the time of receiving the retribution, there will ultimately be no such [worldly] retribution.

(30) Once, in the kingdom of India, there were two poor men who maintained their livelihood through frugal means, constantly selling curd to sustain themselves. The two of them each placed a jar of curd upon their heads and went to the market intending to sell it.
At that time, it was raining and the roads were slippery with mud. A man of wisdom thought to himself:

"Today, because of the muddy rain, the roads are difficult to traverse; I might fall over and break my jar, losing everything inside. If I pour out all the ghee now, even if I should fall, what I lose will be little."

One man of little intelligence took the entire amount and went to the market; midway, on a muddy and slippery road, both men fell down. One man was filled with grief and wept as he rolled upon the ground, while the other showed no sign of sorrow and felt no regret at all.
Someone asked:

"The two of you both broke the jars of curd, and what was lost is equal; there is no difference between you. Why does one person alone weep with tears and lament in distress, while the other remains silent and shows no sign of resentment?"
One person replied, "The curd I was carrying had not yet yielded butter; today the jar broke and my entire supply was lost. For this reason, my grief and resentment are more than I can bear."
One person replied:
"The curd I was carrying has already yielded butter; although the jar is now broken, what has been lost is but little, and for this reason I remain composed and feel no regret."
The jar is a metaphor for the body, and the ghee is a metaphor for wealth and possessions.

There are those who are stingy and greedy, begrudging their wealth and seeking only immediate profit while failing to contemplate impermanence; thus, when the jar of the body suddenly breaks, all their wealth and possessions are lost.
It is like a person who, having lost their butter or curd, is filled with distress and regret, yet remorse comes too late to be of avail.

There is another who has deep faith in the retribution of future lives; he bestows all his wealth and possessions in charity, so that although his physical vessel may perish, he loses very little in the end.
It is also like that man whose jar of curd was broken; though it was damaged, what he lost was very little, and his mind remained composed without any regret.

(31) Once there were five hundred merchants who boarded a ship and entered the sea seeking precious treasures. They encountered a makara fish that raised its head and opened its mouth, intending to devour living beings.
At that time, there was little wind, yet the ship moved as swiftly as an arrow; the caravan leader said to the multitude, "The ship is moving too fast;
we should lower the sails and let her sink."
Immediately, as he had said, they lowered the sails and descended; the ship sped away even faster and could not be stopped.
The caravan leader asked those on the upper deck, "What do you see?"
“I see two suns above, white mountains below, and black mountains in between.
The caravan leader was startled and said, “This is a great fish; what shall we do?”

"We and you have now encountered this dire calamity; having entered the belly of this fish, there is no possibility of survival. Each of you should single-mindedly seek deliverance according to that which you serve.

Thereupon, the multitude each followed their respective objects of veneration, taking refuge with one-pointed devotion to seek escape from this peril. As their prayers grew more earnest, the ship moved faster and faster; in a mere moment, it could not stop and was on the verge of entering the fish's mouth.
Thereupon, the caravan leader addressed the people, saying:
"I have a Great Divinity whose name is Buddha; each of you should abandon what you formerly worshipped and invoke him with a single mind."
Then the five hundred people together raised their voices and cried out, "Namo Buddha! Hearing the name of the Buddha, the fish reflected to himself:
"Today there is once again a Buddha in the world; how could I bear to harm living beings?"
As soon as he had thought this, he immediately closed his mouth; the water all flowed backward and moved far away from the fish’s mouth, and the five hundred merchants were liberated at once.

This fish had previously been a practitioner of the Way; due to his transgressions, he received this fish body. Having heard the name of the Buddha, he immediately recalled his past lives, and thus, through his reflection, a virtuous mind was instantly born within him.

This clarifies that even five hundred merchants, by simply focusing their minds on the Buddha and briefly reciting his name, immediately attained liberation from a calamity as vast as the heavens; how much more so for those who receive and uphold the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi), which causes heavy sins to be lightened and light ones to be extinguished—such a response is hardly to be considered extraordinary.

32. (Thirty-two) When the kalpa is consumed by fire and all is empty, through the power of the causes and conditions of the merit of sentient beings, winds arrive from the ten directions. These winds follow one after another and are able to sustain a great mass of water. Upon this water is a being with a thousand heads and two thousand hands and feet, named Vairambha.

From the navel of this person, a thousand-petaled golden lotus flower emerges; its light is brilliantly radiant, like ten thousand suns shining together, and within the flower sits a person in the full lotus posture.
This person further possesses immeasurable radiance and is named Brahmā Deva-rāja.
He gave birth to eight sons from his mind, and these eight sons produced the heavens, the earth, and the people.
This Brahmā Deva-rāja has exhausted all lust and anger, leaving nothing remaining.
For this reason it is said:

"If there is someone who cultivates pure conduct through dhyāna and eliminates lustful desire, they are said to be practicing the Brahma-path; the turning of the Dharma-wheel by the Buddha is also called the Brahma-wheel."

Since this Brahmā King sits upon a lotus flower, for that reason all Buddhas, in accordance with worldly convention, sit cross-legged upon precious lotus flowers and preach the six pāramitās. Those who hear this Dharma will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

33 (Thirty-three): Once there was a woman of noble birth, whose countenance was upright and whose appearance was exceptionally distinguished; she left the household life to practice and study, attaining the path of Arhatship.

As she was walking alone among the trees outside the city, she encountered a man on the road who, seeing that the bhikṣuṇī’s appearance was upright and beautiful, felt a deep attachment toward her. He stood before her and made a vow, saying:
"If you do not comply with me, I will not allow you to go."
The bhikṣuṇī then explained to her the dharma of the impurity of bodily secretions: "What is there to be craved in the head, eyes, hands, or feet?
That man then said to the bhikṣuṇī, "I love your beautiful eyes."
Then that bhikṣuṇī, with her right hand, gouged out one of his eyes and showed it to the man; as blood flowed down his face, the man’s lustful desire immediately subsided upon seeing it.
The bhikṣuṇī grasped one eye in her hand, returned to the place where the Buddha was, restored the eye to its original position, and related everything in detail to the Buddha.
Consequently, a precept was established: from that time forward, it was not permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to reside outside the city walls or to travel alone outside the village.
34. (34) All the grasses and trees in the world can serve as medicine; it is simply because those who lack the skill of discernment do not recognize them.

Formerly, there was a holy king of physicians named Jīvaka, who could compound medicinal herbs and manifest in the form of a youth; all who saw him were filled with joy, and their various ailments were all healed.

Sometimes a single herb cures many ailments, and sometimes many herbs cure a single ailment; there is no herb in the world that cannot be employed, and there is no ailment in the world that cannot be cured.
When Jīvaka passed away, all the medicinal herbs in the world wept and wailed at once, crying out in unison:
"We can all be used to treat illnesses, yet only Jīvaka was able to understand us."

"After Jīvaka has died, there will be no one again who can clearly understand my methods. Later generations might misapply them, or increase or decrease them so that illnesses are not cured, leading all people in the world to say that I am not divine. It is because I reflect upon this that I weep."
There was only one *harītakī* fruit; standing apart by himself, he did not weep, saying: "I am able to cure all manner of illnesses.
Those who take me shall surely be healed, while those who do not take me will not be cured of their own accord. There is no need for others to recognize my merit, and that is why I do not weep."
