Jīvaka is like the Buddha; the various medicinal herbs are like the various dharmas; and the harītakī is like impermanence (*anityatā*).

This means that when the Buddha was in the world, he skillfully employed the Dharma as medicine to cure the illnesses of people—namely lust, anger, and delusion—as well as other wholesome dharmas, applying them according to what was appropriate.
Having established the principle of impermanence, it is like a skilled physician for the sick.

After the Buddha has passed into extinction, there are few who can skillfully employ all dharmas to transform them according to the occasion. Contemplation of impermanence cures many ailments; it can cure lust, it can cure anger, and it can cure delusion. One who employs it skillfully eliminates the disease, while one who does not employ it skillfully remains unharmed. Therefore, it is likened to the harītakī fruit.

The remaining dharmas are not easily applied; those who employ them must certainly obtain a teacher. One who employs them skillfully will diminish their afflictions, whereas one who does not employ them skillfully will increase their afflictions.
35. Once there was a butcher who went to King Ajātaśatru and begged for a single boon.
The king asked, "What boon do you seek?"
He replied, "At the time of the King’s festival assembly, it is customary to slaughter animals; I pray that Your Majesty grant me permission, and I shall perform all the necessary tasks.
The King said:
“Slaughter is something that people do not delight in; why do you wish to take pleasure in doing it?
He replied, “In the past, when I was a poor man, I supported myself by means of a sheep-slaughterer’s stall; because of this, I was reborn above the Four Heavenly Kings.”
Having exhausted the lifespan of that heaven, he was reborn among humans and continued slaughtering sheep; after his death there, he was reborn in the second heaven.
In this manner, he slaughtered sheep six times, and because of these deeds, he was born throughout all six heavens, receiving immeasurable merit. For this reason, he now begs from the King.
The king asked, "If it were as you say, how would one know it? He replied:
"I remember my past lives.
When the king heard this, he did not believe it and called it a falsehood, saying, "How could such a lowly person as this know his past lives?
Later, he questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha replied:
"It is indeed as you have said; it is no false word.

In a previous life, this person encountered a Pratyekabuddha. Upon seeing the Buddha, he was filled with joy and observed him with a sincere mind: looking up at his head and down at his feet, a virtuous mind immediately arose within him. By virtue of this merit, he has been reborn six times in the heavens of the Six Desire Heavens."

Having been reborn among humans, he naturally recognizes his past lives; because his merit has matured, he has attained this state. Although he has undergone six cycles of birth among devas and humans, his transgressions have not yet matured, and thus he has not yet fully experienced their retribution.
"When this body perishes, you shall fall into hell to undergo the retribution for slaughtering sheep; once that period in hell has ended, you must be reborn among sheep to repay the debt one by one.

Because this man’s knowledge of past lives was shallow, seeing only what occurred within the six heavens and failing to reach back to his seventh previous existence, he concluded that slaughtering sheep was the very cause for birth in heaven.
In this way, one merely recognizes past lives; it is neither a supernormal power (*abhijñā*) nor true insight (*vidyā*).

(36) Once there was a king who deeply understood the nature of sin and merit and believed in the retribution of karmic results. He constantly delighted in practicing generosity and never went against the wishes of others; his fame spread far and wide, such that there was no one who did not hear of him.
At that time, a neighboring state raised an army to attack his kingdom. The king reflected to himself:
"If I go out to battle, there will surely be injury and slaughter; it would be better for me to lose my own life than to wrong my people."
When that army had arrived and entered through the eastern gate of the city, the king departed through the western gate and fled alone into the forest wilderness.
At that time, a certain brāhmaṇa came from a distant land; traveling by way of the woods, he encountered the king. Immediately, the two men greeted one another, and the king asked the brāhmaṇa:
"From where have you come, and where do you intend to go?"
The brahmin said, "I have heard that King So-and-so is devoted to the practice of giving and does not refuse the requests of others; therefore, I have come from afar wishing to ask for something."
The king immediately replied,
"I myself am the one of whom you speak.
Upon hearing this, the brāhmaṇa was struck with wonder and asked the king:
“Your Majesty, why is it that you have become like this?
At that time, the king related the circumstances of the matter in detail to the brāhmaṇa.
Upon hearing this, the brāhmaṇa fell to the ground in a faint and died; after a long while, the king raised him up and sprinkled water upon him, whereupon he finally revived.
The king asked him,
"For what reason is it thus?
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"Since ancient times I have been poor and destitute of wealth; therefore, I came from afar wishing to beg for riches and treasures. How is it that today I have encountered such a king?
Thus I am so distressed that I cannot endure it."
The king then consoled the brahmin: "Do not grieve;
I shall cause you to obtain great wealth and treasure.

Although that foreign king has seized my kingdom, he has not yet captured my person. He has issued a proclamation far and wide offering a very heavy reward for me. You may simply bind me and deliver me to the king’s gate; the king will be delighted and will surely grant you a generous reward."
Thereupon, the brahmin did exactly as he had been told; he bound the man’s two hands with a rope of grass and led him to the king’s gate.

When the gatekeeper saw him, he quickly entered and informed the king. Upon hearing this, the king was both surprised and delighted, and immediately commanded the officer at the gate to bring the person who had seized the royal personage, along with the brahmin, before the king’s seat.
The king asked the brahmin,
"What incantation do you possess that can bring this man here?
The brahmin replied:
“I have no other skill; this man was formerly a king whose heart delighted in giving, and so he has come from afar wishing to beg for something.
While we encountered one another among the trees of the forest, he asked me:
‘Where do you wish to go?’”
At that time, I replied:
"I wish to go to the place of such-and-such a king.
He answered me, saying:
"The king of such-and-such a country was my very self.
Upon hearing these words, I immediately died and was not conscious of it myself; they helped me up and sprinkled water upon me, and asked me again:
"For what reason have you come to this place?"

I replied: "Because I did not practice generosity in past lives, I was born into poverty in this world; therefore, I have come from afar wishing to beg for wealth and treasures, and because my original vow has not been fulfilled, I am merely distressed within myself."
He addressed me with these words of encouragement:
"Do not harbor thoughts of constraint; I shall provide my own body for whatever you require.
Then he spoke to me again:
"You may take a rope and bind my two arms, then deliver me to the king's gate; that king shall surely grant you a reward.
When the king heard the brahmin’s words, he immediately shed tears, rose from his seat, and sat lower before the original king, saying:
"You are a true king of men; I am but a thief."
Thereupon, he gathered his retinue and returned to his own country; the former king was restored to his throne and allowed to govern as before.

This clarifies that when a bodhisattva was originally an ordinary person, such were the deeds of his supreme virtue. If anyone writes out or maintains this scripture with such sincere devotion, neither devas nor malevolent beings shall ever find an opportunity to harm them.
There are two kinds of thieves: first, those who rely on physical strength;
second, those who rely on skillful means.

As for the thief who relies on physical strength, he personally digs through a wall, fashioning it into the shape of a lion’s head or a lotus flower. Having entered the house to take goods, he does not carry everything away but leaves behind a small portion, desiring that the owner may still have enough to live upon, and wishing to make people say, "This is a fine thief."

He then changed his clothes and went together with the others to the house where the property had been lost; when the people there saw the place where the thief had tunneled through the wall, they all said, "This is a clever thief."
At that time, there was a crafty thief disguised as a humble Brahmin who was also among them, and he spoke thus:
"These are not skillful thieves; they expend much effort yet obtain little. How can this be called skill?"
"To obtain many things without exerting effort—that alone constitutes skill.
At that time, the thief Handala took these words to heart; he waited for the crowd to depart and then followed them, asking, "What is meant by a 'skillful thief'?"
He replied, "If you wish to know, simply follow me; within more than a month, I shall cause you to see.
Thereupon, the thief used a stratagem and disguised himself in the garb of a brahmin; he went to the house of a very wealthy elder and said to him:
"I require a small amount of goods; would it not be well if you could give it to me?
At that time, the elder asked for the price of a single robe, whereupon [the man] immediately replied, "I shall provide it to you."
Before he had obtained it, he went back again and said,
"Is the intention you previously promised me certain to be fulfilled? The elder replied:
"I shall ensure that he definitely pays.
Having said this three times, he then drew up a document and went to the authorities to report:
"The householder so-and-so owes me one hundred thousand taels of gold but refuses to repay it."
The bandits then took the elder’s enemy and passed him off as a witness; the local authorities arrested both the witness and the elder, and questioned the witness, saying: "Is it true?"
The people of the time replied, "It is indeed so.

The official then ordered the elder to deliver gold to this brahmin; thus, through a clever stratagem, the thief obtained a great amount of property without the use of physical force. It is the same with sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
37 (37) There are dragons capable of raining down a single drop of water upon a single country, or two, or three, even up to raining over an entire Jambudvīpa.
The dragon thought to himself:
"I wish to hide this single drop of water so that it remains forever and does not dry up;
where could such a place be found? Thus he reflected.
"It cannot be kept in other places; only by placing it within the great ocean will it not dry up.
This is a metaphor for how a small gift can yield an infinite and great reward: it is only when one places it within the path of the Buddha that this occurs.
This clarifies that because the drops of water merge with the dragon’s wisdom, the place they rely upon does not dry up.
Because giving merges with *prajñā*, the place where it is established does not become exhausted.

38. As for why a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) obtains the Golden Wheel: Śakra constantly commands the Four Heavenly Kings to tour the world six days each month to observe the good and evil of people.

The Four Heavenly Kings, along with their princes and messengers, seeing that there was a great king who governed the world through the ten wholesome paths and the four immeasurables, and who was concerned for all people with a mind like that of a compassionate father, reported these matters to Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
Upon hearing this, Śakra rejoiced at his ability to do so and immediately commanded Viśvakarman to bestow upon him a golden wheel.
Viśvakarman then produced the golden wheel and presented it to King Vaiśravaṇa.
The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa entrusted it to a flying yakṣa, who brought it to the great king. The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa commanded this yakṣa:
"You must always carry this golden wheel for the king; you shall not abandon it midway until the end of his life, keeping it above the king's crown."
This yakṣa constantly held it for him, following the noble king’s intentions in his every movement—whether advancing, halting, coming, or going.
When its lifespan was exhausted, he returned it to King Vaiśravaṇa; King Vaiśravaṇa entrusted it to Viśvakarman, who then placed it back within the treasure-store.

39 (Thirty-nine): In the past, there was a Great Brahmā King named Bhaga. Because he had cultivated the causes and conditions for long life in his previous lives, his lifespan lasted for seventy-two Brahmā-heaven human years. Since his lifespan was not exhausted even after its conclusion, he gave rise to a false view on account of that longevity, claiming that he was eternal.
He further thought: "I have attained mastery;
from this day forward, no one shall be able to see me falsely. If I permit it, they shall see me; if I do not permit it, they shall cease."

The Buddha, with his divine mind and the eye of the Way, perceived the Brahma King’s thoughts. Together with his four great disciples—Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahākauṣṭhila—he ascended into the air and sat upon the Brahma King’s head; Śāriputra was on the right, Maudgalyāyana on the left, Mahākāśyapa in front, and Mahākauṣṭhila behind.
He addressed the Brahma King, saying: “You consider yourself one who constantly possesses sovereign mastery; how then can I now sit upon your head?”
He asked again,
"What have you seen such that you consider yourself to always possess mastery? Brahmā replied:
"In my Brahma-heaven, seventy-two beings have successively reached the end of their lifespans, yet I alone have not perished.
Furthermore, three other celestial beings of great merit and virtue have passed away, yet I alone have not perished."
"For this reason, you claim that [the self] is eternal.
The Buddha said to the Brahma King:

"I am the Omniscient One; I see when you were first born and I also see when you will die. Regarding all phenomena, there is no error or delusion; do not be deluded and falsely consider yourself to be eternal."
"This Brahmā King also possesses knowledge of past lives; do you wish to know for certain when he will attain Buddhahood?
He then addressed the Buddha, saying, "Buddha, you know by what causes and conditions I obtained this life span."
The Buddha said to the Brahma King:

"In a former life, you were once a seer possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*). You saw a multitude of people boarding a ship to enter the sea; suddenly a violent wind arose and the waves surged to the heavens. By means of your power as a seer, you rescued these people and brought them ashore, enabling them to escape the calamity of death—this was the first causal condition."

Furthermore, you were once a minister of a great kingdom. There was a village that had violated the king’s law, and at that time the king was so enraged that he intended to execute the entire village. You then took pity on them and exhausted your family's wealth to provide them with a place of refuge, enabling them to be fully saved; this is the second causal condition.
"By these two causes and conditions, you have attained this long life; however, after another thirty-six kalpas, your lifespan shall come to an end.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the Brahma King immediately conceived faith; with single-minded contemplation, he attained the stage of Anāgāmin.

If even this Brahma King attains such a lifespan through these causes and conditions, how much more so for the Buddha, who throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas has accumulated great vows out of compassion for sentient beings—seeking his own head to give to those seeking a head, seeking his own eyes to give to those seeking eyes, and being able to provide everything that is requested until all needs are fully met. His body filling the entirety of space would not be considered great, and a lifespan lasting for as many kalpas as there are motes of dust would not be considered long.
The Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables Spoken by the Buddha
